title: Directors, Coaches, and Editors: The Human Role in the Age of AI
author: Anthea Roberts

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source broadly supports the cluster’s human-led collaboration and work-redesign proposition by predicting that human–AI collaboration will persist while its form evolves. However, it offers no evidence or detail on selective deployment, verification, user expertise, or operating-model redesign.
qs: Human-AI Collaboration will continue, but the nature of this collaboration is likely to change over time.

kp.k: Human guidance shapes AI output quality
kp.d: Roberts presents a cross-domain argument, rather than a legal-sector study, that humans act as directors, coaches and editors of AI. Drawing on her experience building tools at Dragonfly Thinking, she argues that prompts, interactive engagement and refinement are central to performance, with collaboration as important as the underlying model. These are experiential and conceptual claims, not reported empirical findings.
qs: At Dragonfly Thinking, I’ve realized that a crucial part of my role is to build tools that direct AI performances.

Generative AI does not generate alone. Instead, it requires human-AI collaboration and the quality of the outputs depends as much on the nature of that collaboration as on the strength of the underlying AI model.
Similarly, AI needs prompts that guide it effectively, interactive engagement to get the best performance, and editing to take its outputs from good to great.

kp.k: Prompt clarity is a substantive guidance skill
kp.d: Roberts asserts that precise direction produces more meaningful AI responses than poorly structured prompting. She invokes Microsoft Deputy CTO Sam Schillace’s maxim as support, rather than presenting a measured comparison of prompt performance.
qs: The quality of AI’s outputs depends on the clarity of the direction it’s given.
A poorly structured prompt leads to bland responses, while a precise one produces meaningful insights.
Ask smart to get smart

kp.k: Industrial mechanisation supplies an analogy for changing human roles
kp.d: Roberts compares AI-related skill changes to the Industrial Revolution’s shift from direct machine operation toward supervision, maintenance and improvement. The analogy frames movement from doing work to directing, coaching and editing as requiring new cognitive skills; it is not evidence of a measured occupational transition.
qs: Just as the Industrial Revolution demanded new skills from workers who had to learn to oversee machinery, today’s AI revolution requires us to develop new cognitive skills.
At first, humans operated early industrial machines directly; over time, they became supervisors and technicians who maintained and improved those systems.
We’re at a similar point with AI, shifting from doing to directing, coaching and editing.

kp.k: Generational skill differences could reshape workplace learning
kp.d: Roberts predicts that younger workers and students may acquire AI-guidance skills faster than older workers, potentially creating either a generational divide or new collaboration. She identifies reverse mentorship as an opportunity and recommends adaptability and reciprocal learning. No adoption data or specific timeframe is supplied.
qs: This new skill set isn’t widely taught yet, but it’s essential.
Young workers and students today are likely to master these AI guidance skills quickly, while older generations may struggle to keep up.

But there’s also an opportunity for reverse mentorship: young employees who quickly master AI tools can teach their supervisors or older colleagues, creating a more collaborative and less hierarchical learning environment.
We need to recognize that these emerging skills will be foundational in the workplace, where adaptability and willingness to learn from one another will be essential.

kp.k: Skipping primary work may threaten expertise formation
kp.d: Roberts raises, rather than resolves, a concern that younger workers might develop supervisory roles without the practical experience needed for judgment. She frames erosion of expertise as a possible consequence of bypassing foundational work, using employee–supervisor and writer–editor relationships as analogies.
qs: Older workers may worry about how younger ones will develop their own skills and judgment without doing the primary work.
How can you be a great supervisor if you have never learned to be a great employee?
How can you be a great editor if you have never toiled at writing drafts?
Might younger workers end up skipping over important steps, leading to a crumbling of expertise over time?

kp.k: More capable AI may shift coaching toward strategic curation
kp.d: Roberts anticipates that increasing AI sophistication could reduce step-by-step human direction and increase selection, evaluation and refinement of generated content. She recommends developing skills combining technical acumen with human intuition. This is a conditional prediction without a specified date, not an observed transition or a claim that human oversight disappears.
qs: As AI becomes more sophisticated, our role will change. We’ll likely shift from directing and coaching to editing.
As AI continues to evolve, however, we may find that the hands-on coaching it requires now will transition to roles focused more on curation.
This shift will mean we’re less involved in guiding every step and more focused on strategic oversight—evaluating and refining AI-generated content to extract meaningful insights.
Our challenge will be to evolve alongside AI, developing skills that balance technical acumen with human intuition.

kp.k: Collaboration may persist while coaching roles reverse
kp.d: Roberts frames the evolution of human roles as changing collaboration rather than human replacement. She argues that success depends on continual adaptation and speculates that AI could eventually coach humans instead of the reverse; she provides no timeframe or evidence for that possibility.
qs: This evolution doesn’t mean AI will replace us; it means that the nature of our collaboration with AI will continue to change.
Success will depend on our ability to adapt, continually refining the art of guidance, selection, and enhancement as AI’s capabilities grow.
One day, the roles may be even be reversed, with the AI coaching us rather than us coaching the AI.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts argues that AI changes human work from primary production toward guidance and refinement, with a further prospective shift toward strategic curation.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain account of human–AI collaboration, not a claim specifically about legal services. Roberts argues that output quality depends on human direction, prompting, interactive engagement, and editing as well as model capability. She predicts that increasingly sophisticated AI will require less step-by-step coaching and more selection, evaluation, and enhancement of its outputs. She frames this as changing collaboration rather than human replacement, and speculates that AI might eventually coach humans. She also predicts uneven generational acquisition of AI guidance skills, identifies possible erosion of expertise when younger workers bypass primary work as an open question, and proposes reverse mentorship as an opportunity rather than an established outcome.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Roberts bases the argument on personal experience, analogies, and a supporting authority reference, rather than reported empirical tests.
pts.d: Roberts draws on her experience building AI-guidance tools at Dragonfly Thinking. She uses directors, coaches, and editors as analogies for human contributions to AI output, and the Industrial Revolution as an analogy for changing worker skills and supervisory roles. She invokes Microsoft Deputy CTO Sam Schillace’s prompting maxim as supporting authority; it is not an independently established result in this article. The document presents no quantitative data, benchmarks, systematic cases, or measured outcomes supporting the generational predictions, prospective expertise loss, or eventual shift to curation and AI coaching humans.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2025 article describes guidance as a current requirement and predicts an undated, capability-dependent transition toward curation.
pts.d: Roberts presents prompting, engagement, and editing as important now, while describing these skills as not yet widely taught. The movement toward less hands-on supervision is conditional on AI becoming more sophisticated. Generational differences are expressed as likely or possible, not inevitable; expertise erosion is raised through questions. Successful adaptation depends on continued learning and combining technical skills with human intuition. The possibility of AI coaching humans is assigned only to 'one day,' with no schedule or capability threshold.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are AI users and tool builders, students, younger and older workers, and workplace supervisors—not specifically lawyers or legal clients.
pts.d: People working with AI are expected to acquire prompting, direction, selection, and refinement skills as their work moves away from direct production. Younger workers and students are predicted to learn AI guidance quickly, while older workers may struggle with adaptation. Supervisors and older colleagues may worry about juniors developing judgment without doing foundational work, but may also learn AI skills from younger employees through reverse mentorship. Roberts suggests this could make workplace learning less hierarchical. She does not identify legal-market segments, quantify employment effects, or predict specific staffing reductions.
